With de: (illi), de quibus audivi et legi et ipse conscripsi,; ; : de ratione dicendi,.—
With acc. and inf.: ut in ordinem se coactum conscriberet, write down, notice that he should be, etc., : omni personae quam dotem suscepisse cum marito conscribitur, .—

With dat.: huic facinori tanto tua mens liberalis conscia esse non debuit,: temeritati et mendacio meo, (quoted in Arus. Mess. p. 220 Lind.): Fabricium quem ... conscium illi facinori fuisse arbitrabatur,: verbis,: coeptis,.— Poet.: sacris nox, Heins.: deliciis meis antra,: conubiis aether, Wagn. N. cr.: gens nascenti conscia Nilo,.—
With in: mihi in privatis omnibus conscius,; so, conscius vestris in lacrimis adfueram,.—*
With de: addit ad extremum, se audisse a Curione his de rebus conscium esse Pisonem,; cf. conscientia, II. A. β.— (ε) With rel.-clause: multis consciis quae gereretur,.—(ζ) Absol.: nec mihi conscius est ullus homo,; ; cf.: fac me consciam,; ; ; cf. ; ; ; .—Poet.: cetera nox et nos et turris conscia novit,: silva,: rubor,—Hence, subst.: conscĭus, i, m., of those who are participants in a crime, conspiracy, etc., a partaker, jointconspirator, accessory, accomplice, confidant, etc., ; ; sq.; : consciorum nomina exponere,: Othonis,: se (sacerdotes Germanorum) ministros deorum, illos (equos) conscios putant (sc. deorum),.—

With gen.: qui (sc. populus Romanus) si alicujus injuriae sibi conscius fuisset, etc.,; so, sibi nullius culpae,: mihi dissimulati in ullā parte judicii,: sibi irae et iracundiae,: sermonis adversus majestatem tuam habiti nullius conscii sumus nobis,: mens sibi recti,; cf. without sibi,: admissae nequitiae,: audacis facti (lupus),.—
With dat.: sibi factis mens,.—
With in: nuila sibi turpi in re,.—
With acc. and inf. as object, : etsi mihi sum conscius, numquam

me nimis cupidum fuisse vitae, ; .—(ε) With rel.- or subj.-clause: cum sibi conscius esset, quam inimicum deberet Caesarem habere,—With adv.: mulieres male sibi consciae,.— Absol.: ego pol, quae mihi sum conscia, hoc certo scio, etc.,: conscia mens ut cuique sua est, etc.,.—Poet.: virtus,.— Constrr. analogous to the Greek: conscius sum mihi benefacienti and benefaciens (σύνοιδα ἐμαυτῷ πεποιηκότι or ποιῶν), are mentioned by P., as much used earlier, but without exs. in proof.—

To follow a model, copy, an authority, example, opinion, etc.; to imitate, adopt, obey, etc.: Chrysippum Diogenes consequens partum Jovis dejungit a fabulā,: eum morem,: alicujus sententiam,: necesse'st consilia consequi consimilia,; so, sententias (principum),: suum quoddam institutum,: exilitatem,: mediam consilii viam,.—
To follow a preceding cause as an effect, to ensue, result, to be the consequence, to arise or proceed from: rebus ab ipsis Consequitur sensus,; ; ; cf. : ex quo fit ut pudorem rubor, terrorem pallor et tremor consequatur, : quam eorum opinionem magni errores consecuti sunt,: quod dictum magna invidia consecuta est,: ex quo illud naturā consequi, ut communem utilitatem nostrae anteponamus,; ; : quia libertatem pax consequebatur,.—
Of a logical sequence, to follow: si quod primum in conexo est, necessarium est, fit etiam quod consequitur necessarium,; ; cf. under P. a.—
Meton. (causa pro effectu), by following after any person or thing, to reach, overtake, come up with, attain to, arrive at.
Lit.
With acc.: si statim navigas, nos Leucade consequere,: aliquem in itinere,; Pompeius ap. , A, § 3: fugientem,; ; ; cf. : cohortes,: virum,: rates, et saep.—

With things as objects (so most freq.), to obtain, acquire, get, attain, reach: ut opes quam maximas consequantur,; cf. quaestum,: amplissimos honores,: magistratum,: eam rem (i. e. regna),: dum sua quisque spolia consequi studet,.—With ab: nec dubitat quin ego a te nutu hoc consequi possem,: ab aliquo suum consequi, Gai ; ; .—With ex: fructum amplissimum ex vestro judicio,: gloriosam victoriam ex rei publicae causā,: aliquid commodi ex laboriosā exercitatione corporis,; .—With per: omnia per senatum (corresp. with adsequi per populum),; . —With abl.: ut omnem gloriam ... omni curā atque industriā consequare,; , b, 2 fin.: suis erga aliquem meritis inpunitatem,: tantam gloriam duabus victoriis,; ; ; ; ; ; .—With in and abl.: si quid in dicendo consequi possum,: in hac pernicie rei publicae ... gratiam,: Achillis gloriam in rebus bellicis,; cf. .—With ut or ne: hoc consequi, ut ne, etc.,: nec legum repertores sine summā vi orandi consecutos, ut. etc.,; ; ; ; ; vix per matrem consecutus, ut, etc., Suet : per quae si consequi potuimus, ut, etc.,: sicut hic Cicero consequitur, ne, etc.,.—Absol.: quibus ex rebus largiter erat consecutus, made great profit, Auct. minuta, quae non possunt oculi consequi, .—

To agree, accord, harmonize with a person or thing; to assert unitedly, determine in common, decree, to unite upon something accordantly, etc. (freq and class. in prose and poetry); constr with cum, inter se, the dat., or absol. of person; and with the acc., de, ad, in, the inf.. causā, or absol. of the thing.

SCIPIONE., etc. (i. e. hunc unum plurimi consentiunt Romanum bonorum optimum fuisse virum ... Lucium Scipionem), inscription of the Scipios, C. I. L. 1, 32: Wordsworth, Fragm, and Spec. p. 160; cf. ; and : omnes mortales unā mente consentiunt, omnia arma eorum, qui haec salva velint, contra illam pestem esse capienda,; so ; ; —With inf.: seu quicquid ubique magnificum est in claritatem ejus (sc. cum: consentire cum aliquā re, verbis discrepare,: cum his (oratoribus) philosophi consentiunt,; so .—With dat.: illis superioribus,; so : sibi ipse,; cf. : cui parti,: iis, quibus delectantur,: studiis alicujus,—With adversus: adversus maleficium omne consensimus,: adversus patrem cum amicis,, ext. 3.—With ad: parvo exercitu, sed ad benevolentiam erga nos consentiente,; ; ; ; ; ; cf.: ad rem publicam conservandam,: ad decernendum triumphum,: ad necem ejus,: ad indutias,.—With in: in homine non, ut omne, omnia in unum consentientia, sed singulis membris suum cuique consilium,: in hoc non contumaciter consentio,; cf.: consentire in asserendā libertate,: puro pioque duello quaerendas censeo itaque consentio consciscoque, old formula of voting in .—With ut: senatus ... censuit consensit conscivit ut bellum cum priscis Latinis fieret, old formula for declaring war,.—With ne: constat, ad alia discordes in uno adversus patrum voluntatem consensisse, ne dicerent dictatorem,.—With acc. rei: consensit et senatus bellum,i. e. has voted, decreed war,: bellum erat consensum,: consensa in posterum diem contio,.—With inf.: si consenserint possessores non vendere, quid futurum est?. —Impers.: de prioribus consentitur,: inter plurimos consensum est duas esse partes,; ; ; so, consensum est, ut, etc.,.—

la:noun:consilium.html:
consĭlĭum, ii, n.
from con and root sal-; Sanscr. sar-; cf. consul
,
deliberation, consultation, a considering together, counsel (cf. concilium; very freq. in all periods and species of composition).
Prop.: consulta sunt consilia,are finished, at an end,: quid in consilio consuluistis? Ritschl: consilium volo capere unā tecum,: neque pol consili locum habeo neque ad auxilium copiam,: cum aliquo consilia conferre, (v. confero, I. B.): saepe in senatu consilia versata sunt,; : quasi vero consilii sit res, et non necesse sit, etc.,as if the matter were yet open for deliberation,; cf. : quid efficere possis, tui consilii est,is for you to consider,: vestrum jam consilium est. non solum meum, quid sit vobis faciendum,: quid aetati credendum sit, quid nomini, magni consilii est, ; cf.: nihil mihi adhuc accidit, quod majoris consilii esset,: in consilio habere,: fit publici consilii particeps,; cf. ; : nocturna,: arcanis ut interesset, et saep.—
Meton.
In abstr.
A conclusion made with consideration, a determination, resolution, measure, plan, purpose, intention, ; cf.: consilium est aliquid faciendi aut non faciendi excogitata ratio,; : certum,: callidum,: ut sunt Gallorum subita et repentina consilia,: aliquid communi consilio agere,: consilium communicaverunt perfeceruntque,: aedificandi consilium abicere,; ; : deponere,.—And of the purpose. as opp. to the act, etc.: quod initio scripsi, totius facti tui judicium non tam ex consilio tuo quam ex eventu homines esse facturos,: quasi exitus rerum, non hominum consilia, legibus vindicentur,: mentem peccare, non corpus, et unde consilium afuerit culpam abesse,. —Often with epithets characterizing the person who forms the purpose, etc.: amentissimum,: audax,; : fortissima cousilia,: fidele,; : providens,: malum,: temerarium,: incautum,: lene,: praeceps,: repudio quod consilium primum intenderam,: eo consilio, uti frumento Caesarem intercluderet,; ; ; : quo consilio huc imus?; also: hoc consilio ut,: privato consilio, on one's own account (opp. publico consilio, in the name or behalf of the state): qui contra consulem privato consilio exercitus comparaverunt,; ; .—Sometimes absol. consilio adverbially, intentionally, designedly: casu potius quam consilio,: consul, seu forte, seu consilio, Venusiam perfugit,; ; .—
Esp. in the phrases,
Consilium capere, to form a purpose or plan, to resolve, decide, determine: neque, quid nunc consili capiam, scio, De virgine istac,: consilium capere with a gen. gerund., ; ; ; ; ; ; 10, 38, 6; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. with gen.: profectionis et reversionis meae,.—With inf., ; ; ; —With ut: capio consilium, ut senatum congerronum convocem,: consilium ceperunt plenum sceleris, ut nomen hujus deferrent,; : consilium cepi, ut antequam luceret exirem,. 10; ; .—And with inf.: consilium cepit ... iter in urbem patefacere,: hominis fortunas evertere,: Heraclius capit consilium ... non adesse ad judicium,: ex oppido profugere,; ; .—
In the same sense, inire consilium, with similar construction: inita sunt consilia urbis delendae,; : regni occupandi consilium inire,; ; : jus gentium cujus violandi causā consilium initum erat,; : sceleris conandi consilia inierat,; : Graeci consilium ineunt interrumpendi pontis,; : iniit consilia reges Lacedaemoniorum tollere,: consilia inibat, quemadmodum, etc.,: de bello consilia inire incipiunt,: cum de recuperandā libertate consilium initum videretur,: consilia inita de regno,: atrox consilium init, ut, etc.,.—
Freq. consilium est, with and without inf., I purpose: ita facere,; ; ; ; ; ; Dietsch. —Rarely with ut: ut filius Cum illà habitet ... hoc nostrum consilium fuit,: ea uti acceptā mercede deseram, non est consilium,; and absol.: quid sui consilii sit, ostendit,.—Hence,
In partic., in milit. lang., a warlike measure, device, stratagem: consilium imperatorium quod Graeci στρατήγημα appellant, ; so ; ; ; cf.: opportunus consiliis locus (= insidiis),.—
With special reference to the person for whose advantage a measure is devised, counsel, advice: tu quidem antehac aliis solebas dare consilia mutua,; so, dare,: quid das consili?: Cethegum minus ei fidele consilium dedisse,: vos lene consilium datis,; et saep.: juvabo aut re aut operā aut consilio bono,; imitated by Ter.: aut consolando aut consilio aut re juvero, (quoted ap. ); cf. ; ; ; : te hortor ut omnia moderere prudentiā tuā, ne te auferant aliorum consilia,: sin aliquid impertivit tibi sui consilii,: consiliis, non curribus utere nostris,: facile ratio tam salubris consilii accepta est,: saniora consilia pati,.—
As a mental quality, understanding, judgment, wisdom, sense, penetration, prudence: et dominari in corpore toto Consilium quod nos animum mentemque vocamus,; : acta illa res est animo virili, consilio puerili,; cf. : ut popularis cupiditas a consilio principum dissideret,: majore studio quam consilio ad bellum proficisci, Dietsch: res forte quam consilio melius gestae,: quae quanto consilio gerantur, nullo consilio adsequi possumus,: simul consilium cum re amisisti?; cf.: miseros prudentia prima relinquit, Et sensus cum re consiliumque fugit,: mulieres omnes propter infirmitatem consilii majores in tutorum potestate esse voluerunt,: vir et consilii magni et virtutis,: cum plus in illo senili animo non consilii modo sed etiam virtutis esse dicerent,; so, tam iners, tam nulli consili Sum,: est hoc principium improbi animi, miseri ingenii, nulli consilii,: omnes gravioris aetatis, in quibus aliquid consilii aut dignitatis fuit,; cf. : misce stultitiam consiliis brevem,: quae res in se neque consilium neque modum Habet ullum, eam consilio regere non potes,. —
Poet., transf., of inanim. things: consilii inopes ignes,indiscreet,: vis consili expers,; .—
In concr., the persons who deliberate, a council; of the Roman senate: senatum, id est orbis terrae consilium, delere gestit,; ; ; : summum consilium orbis terrae,; ; ; : di prohibeant, ut hoc, quod majores consilium publicum vocari voluerunt, praesidium sectorum existimetur,i. e. a court of justice,; cf.: qui ex civitate in senatum propter dignitatem, ex senatu in hoc consilium delecti estis propter severitatem,.—Of the division of the centumviri, who sat for ordinary cases in four consilia: sedebant centum et octoginta judices, tot enim quattuor consiliis colliguntur,: omnibus non solum consiliis sed etiam sententiis superior discessit,: Galba consilio celeriter convocato sententias exquirere coepit,a council of war,; cf.: consilio advocato,; : castrense,: mittunt (Carthaginienses) triginta seniorum principes: id erat sanctius apud illos consilium,; cf. : consilium Jovis,: bonorum atque sapientium,—
Facetiously: paulisper tace, Dum ego mihi consilia in animum convoco, et dum consulo,.—
(Acc. to II. A.

1. c.) A counsellor: ille ferox hortator pugnae consiliumque fuit,: Clymene, Aethraque, Quae mihi sunt comites consiliumque duae, (17), 268; .

la:verb:consisto.html:
con-sisto, stĭti, stĭtum, 3,
v. n., to place one's self anywhere, to stand still, stand, halt, stop, make a stop (very freq. and class. in prose and poetry).
Lit.
In gen.: jam hunc non ausim praeterire, quin consistam et conloquar,: otiose nunc jam ilico hic consiste,: ubi ad ipsum veni diverticulum, constiti,; cf. : uti et viatores consistere cogant,: neque is (Demosthenes) consistens in loco, sed inambulans atque ascensu ingrediens arduo,: si ludius constitit aut tibicen repente conticuit,; cf. : plura scribam ad te cum constitero: nunc eram plane in medio mari,: constitit nusquam primo quam ad Vada venit, Brut. ap. : in quibus oppidis consistere praetores et conventum agere solebant,: Romae post praeturam,, § 101: ire modo ocius, interdum consistere,: in muro consistendi potestas erat nulli,: omnes ordines, tota in illā contione Italia constitit,: ad mensam consistere et ministrare,; so, ad aras,: ad ramos,: ante domum,: ante torum,: in aede,: in medio,; and with a simple abl.: limine,; 9, 397; ; : post eum,: in pedes,: calce aliquem super ipsum debere consistere,trample on,.—
In partic.
To set, become hard or solid: frigore constitit Ister,has been frozen,; cf. unda,: sanguis, Poët. ap. Cic. Tusc. 2, 17, 38: alvus,; ; cf.: cum jam perfecte mustum deferbuit et constitit,: album ex ovo, quo facilius consistat,.—
Cum aliquo, to station or place one's self with some one for conversation, to stand with: in hoc jam loco cum altero Constitit,; : cum hoc consistit, hunc amplexatur,.—
To take one's place, take position, assume a place or attitude for an action, etc.; of a musician: ut constitit,; of an actor: in scaenā vero postquam solus constitit,; of an orator: in communibus suggestis,: Aesopus mediā subito in turbā constitit,; for shooting: post acer Mnestheus adducto constitit arcu,; cf. of athletes, etc.,; : inter duas acies,: cum aliquo,.—Hence,
Milit. t. t., to halt, make a halt, take a position, to make a stand (opp. to a march, flight, or disorder): locus, ubi constitissent,: qui in superiore acie constiterant,; cf.: in sinistrā parte acies,: in fluctibus,: sub muro,: juxta, al.: pro opere,: equites Ariovisti pari intervallo constiterunt,: constitit utrumque agmen,: sic regii constiterant, et saep.: ut reliquae (legiones) consistere non auderent,: in locis superioribus consistere,: a fugā,: naves eorum nostris adversae constiterunt,.—
Jurid. t. t., to appear as accuser before a court of justice: cum debitoribus,: cum matre,: adversus dominos,.—
Poet.: fert animus propius consistere,i. e. take a nearer view,.—
To have a stand as a dealer, occupy a place of business: ede ubi consistas,: in tabernā, Müll.: IN SCHOLA,; cf.: locum consistendi Romanis in Galliā non fore,; .—
Trop.
In gen., to rest, remain, stand, ; cf. : patiamini eo transire illius turpitudinis infamiam, ubi cetera maleficia consistunt,; cf.: ut unde orta culpa esset, ibi poena consisteret,: ante oculos rectum pietasque pudorque constiterant,. —
In partic.
To pause, to dwell upon, delay, stop: in uno nomine,: ipsa mihi veritas manum inicit et paulisper consistere et commorari cogit,; cf. : in singulis,.—Impers. pass.: ista quae spectantur, ad quae consistitur,.—
(Acc. to I. B. 2.) To be or remain firm, unshaken, immovable, steadfast, to be at rest, to stand one's ground, to continue, endure, subsist, be, exist: mente consistere,; so, neque mente nec linguā neque ore,: praeclare in forensibus causis,: in dicendo,: verbo quidem superabis me ipso judice, re autem ne consistes quidem ullo judice,; cf. of the cause itself: quia magistratus aliquis reperiebatur, apud quem Alfeni causa consisteret,; cf. also: modo ut tibi constiterit fructus otii tui,: in quo (viro) non modo culpa nulla, sed ne suspitio quidem potuit consistere,; cf. : confiteor ... me consistere in meo praesidio sic, ut non fugiendi hostis sed capiendi loci causā cessisse videar,: vitam consistere tutam,to remain, continue safe, Lachm. N. cr.: constitit in nullā qui fuit ante color,: sunt certi denique fines, Quos ultra citraque nequit consistere rectum,; : quales cum vertice celso Aëriae quercus constiterunt,: nullo in loco, nullā in personā ... consistunt (ista quae vires atque opes humanae vocantur),, ext. 7: spes est hunc miserum aliquando tandem posse consistere, to take a firm stand (the figure derived from fleeing soldiers), : si prohibent consistere vires,.—*
Cum aliquo, to agree with: videsne igitur Zenonem tuum cum Aristone verbis consistere, re dissidere, cum Aristotele et illis re consentire, verbis discrepare, .—
In gen., to be, exist: vix binos oratores laudabiles constitisse,: sine agricultoribus nec consistere mortales nec ali posse manifestum est,, praef. § 6; : quadringentis centum Venerios non posse casu consistere,to occur, lake place, be thrown,: summa studia officii inter nos certatim constiterunt, Lentul. ap. : sed non in te quoque constitit idem Exitus, take or have place, .—
With in, ex, or the simple abl. (in Quint. also with circa and inter;v.infra), to consist in or of, to depend upon: major pars victūs eorum in lacte, caseo, carne consistit,: omnis per se natura duabus Constitit in rebus,: e quibus haec rerum summa consistat,; so with ex, ; ; with abl.: deveniunt in talis disposturas, Qualibus haec rerum consistit summa,; ; : vita omnis in venationibus atque in studiis rei militaris consistit,: in eo salus et vita optimi cujusque consistit,: in hoc summa judicii causaque tota consistit,; cf. : causam belli in personā tuā,: in quibus vita beata,: in unā honestate omne bonum,: in nomine controversia,; : in actu rhetoricen,; : spes omnis consistebat Datami in se locique naturā,.—With abl., : omnis quaestio circa res personasque consistere videtur,; : quaestio inter utile atque honestum consistet,. —
As opp. to progressive motion, to come to a stand, stand still, stop, rest, take rest, cease: sola Ubi quiesco, omnis familiae causa consistit tibi,: omnis administratio belli consistit,: vel concidat omne caelum omnisque terra consistat necesse est,: forensium rerum labor et ambitionis occupatio constitisset,: usura,: διάρροια, ; cf.: videndum, morbus an increscat, an consistat, an minuatur,remains unchanged,; and: cursus pituitae,: cum ad Trebiam terrestre constitisset bellum,: cum bellum Ligustinum ad Pisas constitisset,; : infractaque constitit ira,: Gaius ejusque posteri in equestri ordine constitere usque ad Augusti patrem,; cf.: maledictum, quod intra verba constitit,stopped at, went no farther than,.!*? Consisto as v. a. = constituo formerly stood ; ; but these passages are corrected in recent editions. It is now found only , a doubtful passage, where Hertz reads: cum ad judices coniiciendae [consistendae] causae gratiā venissent.

con-sīdĕro, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.

Lit.: contemplari unum quidque otiose et considerare coepit,: candelabrum etiam atque etiam,, § 65: argentum (with contemplari),, § 33: opus (pictorum),: aliquem,: pallium diligentius,; cf. : feminas diligenter ac lente mercantium more,: formam, quā ludum gladiatorium erat aedificaturus,: lucentia sidera,: spatium, —

With a rel.-clause: num tamen exciderit ferrum considerat, hastae,.—

With acc.: mecum in animo vitam tuam,; so, eos casus mecum ipse,: reliquum est, quod ipsae optime considerabitis, vestri similes feminae sintne Romae,: res atque pericula nostra,: simul ipse qui suadet considerandus est,.— With ex: Rosciorum factum ex ipsius Chrysogoni judicio,. —With aliquid ex aliquā re: aliquid ex se et ex suā naturā,; .—

a union, association (several times in Cic.; elsewhere rare): consociatio hominum atque communitas,; cf. ; 1, 41, 149: gentis,: sinistra siderum, Firm. 6, 12 fin.

la:verb:conspicio.gloss: to see, watch, observe, perceive, catch sight of, look at with admiration or close attention, gaze upon, contemplate, behold, espy
senses: to see, watch, observe, perceive, catch sight of, look at with admiration or close attention, gaze upon, contemplate, behold, espy
to attract attention, to be conspicuous, to be visible
la:verb:conspicio.html:
con-spĭcĭo, spexi, spectum, 3, v. a. and n.,
to look at attentively, to get sight of, to descry, perceive, observe (class. in prose and poetry).
Lit.
In gen.
Absol.: inter eas regiones, quā oculi conspiciant, Müll.: in tabernam,.—
With acc.: me interrogas, Qui ipsus equidem nunc primum istanc tecum conspicio semul,: quae aedes ... quas quotiensquomque conspicio, fleo,: si queat usquam Conspicere amissum fetum,: quandoque te in jure conspicio, Leg. Act. ap. , and : ut procul novum vehiculum Argonautarum e monte conspexit,: quisque ... quae prima signa conspexit, ad haec constitit,: quos cum apud se in castris Ariovistus conspexisset,: ubi primum nostros equites conspexerunt,; 2, 26: sidus in regione caeli, etc.,: qui lucus ex insulā conspiciebatur,: conspici inter se,to be visible to one another,: cum inter se conspecti essent,: hunc simulac cupido conspexit lumine virgo,: conspectis luminibus crebris,: locum insidiis conspeximus ipsi,: quae mihi tunc primum, tunc est conspecta supremum,: super tabernaculum ... unde ab omnibus conspici posset, imago Solis fulgebat,: conspecto delatore ejus,: rugas in speculo,: cornua in undā,: arcem,: scopulum,.—Of an inanimate subject: si illud signum (Jovis) solis ortum et forum curiamque conspiceret,.—With two accus., when an action, condition, etc., is the object: quam (matrem) paucis ante diebus laureatam in suā gratulatione conspexit, eandem, etc. ... eundem (filium) spoliatum omni dignitate conspiciat,: strata volgi pedibus detrita viarum Saxea,: superiora loca multitudine armatorum completa,: quos laborantes,: aliquos ex nave egredientes,: aliquem conspiciens ad se ferentem,: naves suas oppletas serpentibus,: (Hannibalem) humi jacentem,: adrasum quendam,; cf., pass.: quamvis non alius flectere equum sciens Aeque conspicitur,: cum interim Metellus, monte degrediens cum exercitu, conspicitur, dub.; v. conspicor: terribilior niger conspicitur (canis),.—
With acc. and inf.: corpus ut exanimum siquod procul ipse jacere Conspicias hominis,: qui nostros victores flumen transisse conspexerant,: centum procurrere currus,; .—
Pregn., to look at with admiration or close attention, to gaze upon, observe, contemplate.
Act.: quid nunc supina sursum in caelum conspicis?: orabat, ne se, quem paulo ante cum egregiā stirpe conspexissent, orbum liberis facerent,: Demetrium ut pacis auctorem cum ingenti favore conspiciebant,: quem cum omnes conspicerent propter novitatem ornatūs ignotamque formam,: cum bene notum Porticus Agrippae te conspexerit,.—
Esp. pass.: conspici, to attract attention, to be conspicuous, noticed, observed, distinguished, admired: inania sunt ista ... delectamenta paene puerorum, captare plausus, vehi per urbem, conspici velle,: in gestu nec

venustatem conspiciendam, nec turpitudinem esse, : sic quisque hostem ferire, murum adscendere, conspici dum tale facinus faceret, properabat,: supellex modica, non multa, ut in neutram partem conspici posset,: quid te ut regium juvenem conspici sinis?: maxime conspectus ipse est, curru equis albis juncto urbem invectus,: vestitus nihil inter aequales excellens, arma atque equi conspiciebantur,; ; : quorum Conspicitur nitidis fundata pecunia villis,: tu formosissimus alto Conspiceris caelo ( = inter deos versaris),: prima bonis animi conspicerere tui,; ; .—Less freq. in an unfavorable sense, to be notorious, to be gazed at with dislike or contempt: carere me adspectu civium quam infestis oculis omnium conspici mallem,: ne quid faciat, quod conspici et derideri posset, Aug. ap. .—

Trop., to perceive mentally, to understand, comprehend: satis in rem quae sint meam ego conspicio mihi,: quantum ego nunc corde conspicio meo,; cf.: ut conspiciatis eum mentibus, quoniam oculis non potestis,: nullus error talis in L. Aemilio Paulo conspectus est,.—Hence,
conspĭcĭens, entis, P. a. (acc. to II. B.), having understanding, intelligent: ad quas (contumelias) despiciendas non sapiente opus est viro, sed tantum conspiciente, Haase (al. consipiente). —
conspectus, a, um, P. a.
(Acc. to I. A. 1.) Visible: tumulus hosti conspectus,; cf. ; : agmina inter se satis conspecta,. —
(Acc. to I. B.) Striking, distinguished, remarkable, gazed at, = conspicuus (perh. not ante-Aug.): Pallas chlamyde et pictis conspectus in armis, (conspicuus, conspicabilis, Serv.); so, victor Tyrio in ostro,; cf. : juventus,: patris avique fama conspectum eum faciebat,: conspectus elatusque supra modum hominis privati,.—Comp., ; ; ; ; —Sup. and adv. apparently not in use.—
conspĭcĭendus, a, um, P. a. (acc. to I. B.), worth seeing, worthy of attention, distinguished (perh. not ante-Aug.): insideat celeri conspiciendus equo,: Nemesis donis meis,: Hyas formā,: mater formosa Inter Dictaeos greges,: eques,: opus vel in hac magnificentiā urbis,; ; .

senses: sight (the ability to see; power of sight)
la:noun:conspectus.html:
conspectus, ūs, m.
conspicio
,
a seeing, looking at, a look, sight, view, the range or reach of sight, the power of seeing (freq., and class. in prose and poetry).
Lit.: casurusne in conspectum videatur animus, an tanta sit ejus tenuitas, ut fugiat aciem, : quo longissime conspectum oculi ferebant,: obscuritas lucis Romanis non adimebat in omnis partes conspectum,: conspectu urbis frui,: suorum,: sese dare in conspectum, ap. : dare se in conspectum alicui,; ; cf.: alicui in conspectum prodire,: prodire ad aliquem in conspectum,; : paene in conspectu exercitūs nostri,before the eyes,: illam e conspectu amisi meo,: venire in conspectum alicujus,; : fugere e conspectu alicujus,; : ex hominum conspectu morte decedere,: fugare aliquem e conspectu,: conspectum fugere,.—
Pregn., public attention, notice: subito consilium cepi ut ante quam luceret exirem, ne qui conspectus fieret aut sermo,—
Meton.
Presence, proximity (very freq.; in many connections coinciding with the foregoing, as the phrase venire in conspectum can be translated to come before the eyes or to come near; so also e conspectu fugere, etc.).
Of persons: etsi scio, eis fore meum conspectum invisum hodie,: (tibi) cujus prope in conspectu Aegyptus est,; so, in conspectu, in the presence or vicinity, before the eyes, before the face of, in sight, ; ; ; .—
Of inanimate things: quercus, quae est in oppidi conspectu,: procul a conspectu imperii,: spectet patriam; in conspectu legum libertatisque moriatur,.—
Appearance (cf. adspectus; very rare): videamus animi partis, quarum est conspectus inlustrior, Madv. ad loc.: Hieronymus ... primo statim aspectu omnia quam disparia essent ostendit,i. e. at the first view the public had of him,; .—
Trop., the mental view, glance, survey, consideration (rare, but in good prose): quae ponunt in conspectu animi, quae cernere et videre non possumus,: et cognitio naturae,: uno in conspectu omnia videre,; ; ; ; : ut ea ne in conspectu quidem relinquantur,never come into consideration, are scarcely observed,.—
In Gellius concr., like the Gr. σύνοψις, a short view, sketch, synopsis, ; .

la:noun:consponsor.html:
con-sponsor, ōris, m.
A joint surety, ; .—
One who binds or obligates himself to something ( = conjurator), acc. to Müll.

la:noun:conspiratio.html:
conspīrātĭo, ōnis, f.
1. conspiro
, prop.
a blowing or breathing together. *
Lit., of unison in wind instruments: canentium,.—Far more freq.,
Trop., an agreement in feeling or opinion, union, unanimity, concord, harmony.
In a good sense: conspiratione hominum atque consensu,: bonorum omnium,: optimatium,: omnium ordinum ad defendendam libertatem (with concordia), Lentul. ap. : (amici) quantā amoris conspiratione consentientis,: conspiratio consensusque virtutum,: in re publicā bene gerendā,: civitatium,. —
In a bad sense, a plotting, plot, mutiny, conspiracy, ; ; ; Brut. ap. , a, 5; ; ; ; et saep.—
Meton., the conspirators, body of conspirators: cum tota ejus conspiratio late quaereretur,.

la:verb:conspiro.html:
con-spīro, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. n., to blow or breathe together, to sound together. *
Lit.: aereaque adsensu conspirant cornua rauco, (et tubae simul inflabantur, Serv.).—Far more freq. and in good prose,
Trop.
To harmonize, agree, accord: conspirans mutuus ardor, * ; cf.: tanta rerum consentiens, conspirans, continuata cognatio,; : consilium omnis vitae consentiens et paene conspirans,; ; : in quibus (operibus) plurium conatus, praeeunte aliquā jucundā voce, conspirat, * : talis ... animus, ut multae in illo artes ... multarum aetatum exempla, sed in unum conspirata,harmoniously blending,.—
To agree together in thought or feeling, to accord, unite, combine.
In a good sense: conligite vos, conspirate nobiscum, consentite cum bonis,: mirabiliter populus Romanus universus et omnium generum ordinumque consensus ad liberandam rem publicam conspiravit,; cf. ; .—Impers.: in commune conspirabatur ab utroque (Cic. Oecon.?) 12 praef. § 8. —
Part.: conspiratus, mid., having agreed, combined; acting in concert: milites legionis VIII. subito conspirati pila conjecerunt, Kraner ad loc.—
In a bad sense, to plot together, to enter into a conspiracy, to conspire (so freq. in the histt. after the Aug. per., esp. in Suet.).
Absol.: priusquam plures civitates conspirarent, Caes. B. G. 3, 10 fin.; ; ; .—
With in and acc.: in injuriam,; : in caedem alicujus,: in necem,: in destinatam mortem,: in facinus,: in Augustum,.—Cf. impers.: conspiratum est in eum a sexaginta amplius,. —*
With ad: ad res novas,.—*
With ut: ut Senatum adorirentur,.—* (ε) With ne: conspirasse corporis partes, ne manus ad os cibum ferrent,.—* (ζ) With inf.: perdere aliquem,.—
Part.: conspīrātus, a, um, having conspired, having entered into a conspiracy: his conspiratis factionum partibus,. —And subst.: conspīrāti, ōrum, m., like conjurati, the conspirators, ; ; ; .— Hence, * conspīrātē, adv., with one accord, unanimously; in comp.: conspiratius ad arma concurrere,.

senses: to observe, notice, catch sight of, spot
la:verb:conspicor.html:
conspĭcor, ātus, 1,
v. dep. a. [id.], to get sight of, to descry, see, perceive (very freq. in Plaut. and Caes.; several times in Ter.; elsewh. rare; never in Lucr., Cic., Virg., or Hor.).
With acc.: nec quemquam conspicor alium in viā,: Epidicumne ego conspicor?; : ante aedis erum meum,; 3, 2, 9: in tenebris conspicatus si sis me,; : (Ajacem) occisum,; ; ; ; * ; : hunc conspicatae naves,.—
With acc. and part.: hic quis est, quem huc advenientem conspicor,: perterritos hostes conspicati,; and 8; .—
With acc. and inf. as object: illam geminos filios pueros peperisse conspicor,; ; ; .—
With rel.-clause: quae res in nostris castris gererentur conspicati,.—(ε) Absol.: contempla et conspicare idem esse apparet, Müll.: cum interim Metellus ... conspicatur, primo dubius quidnam insolita facies ostenderet, Dietsch; Jacobs ad loc. (where MSS. have conspicitur, v. conspicio, I. A. β; but cf. Don. ad ).!*? Pass., to be seen: ut nunc paupertas conspicatur (θεωρεῖται), Varr. ap. P.

senses: striking, conspicuous, distinguished, illustrious, remarkable (attracting attention)
la:adj:conspicuus.html:
conspĭcŭus, a, um, adj.
1. conspicio
(poet. or in post-Aug. prose, esp. in Tac.; not in Quint.).
Lit., that is or comes in view, visible; opp. occultus: quot inter Occultum stellae conspicuumque polum,: rebus ab auditis conspicuisque,: late vertex, * : signum in proeliis,: acies barbarorum,: tabernaculum undique,: sidus omnibus e terris, Augustus ap. .—
Trop., in gen.: habere mortem in conspicuo,before the eyes,: nives,: pyramides,.—
Pregn., that attracts the attention to itself, striking, conspicuous, distinguished, illustrious, remarkable, φανερός; with dat. pers.: Romanis conspicuum eum novitas divitiaeque faciebant,; .—With abl.: insignis clara conspicuusque domo,; so ; ; ; ; ; ; cf. with dat. pers.: consilio, manu, voce insignis hosti, conspicuus suis,.—Absol.: ambo conspicui,; so ; ; ; .

la:verb:conspergo.html:
conspergo (in MSS. also conspar-go; cf. 1. aspergo), si, sum, 3, v. a.
spargo
.
To sprinkle, moisten, besprinkle, bespatter, strew (very freq. and class.).
Lit.
With acc. and abl.: fores vino,: aras multo sanguine,: terram tabo,: me lacrimis,: carnem sale,: terram rore,: semen cinere,: tracta placentae farinae L. II. (i. e. libris duabus),—Poet.: herbas viridantes floribus,: caput Tauri stellis frequentibus,.—
Without abl.: consperge (humum) ante aedes,; cf.: humum aestuantem,: vias propter pulverem,—
Trop. of oratorical ornament, to besprinkle or strew, to cover (the image taken from flowers): (oratio) conspersa sit quasi verborum sententiarumque floribus,: quae quādam hilaritate conspersimus,; * .—
To scatter, sprinkle: vinum vetus, dub.

senses: to stand still; to remain the same; stand firm
to be established, well known, understood, clear
to consist, to be composed of
la:verb:consto.html:
con-sto, stĭti, stātum (constātūrus, ; ; ; ; Lact. Opif. Dei, 7, 11), 1, v. n.
To stand together, stand with some person or thing.
Lit. (very rare): constant, conserunt sermones inter se drapetae,.—
Trop., to stand with, to agree with, be in accord or agreement, to correspond, fit.
With cum and abl. (cf. consisto, II. B. 3.): considerabit, constetne oratio aut cum re aut ipsa secum,: sententiā non constare cum superioribus et inferioribus sententiis, etc.,.—
Absol.: veri similis narratio erit, si spatia temporum, personarum dignitates, consiliorum rationes, locorum opportunitates constabunt,.—
With dat.: si humanitati tuae constare voles,.—And esp. with sibi, to agree, accord with itself, to remain like one's self, be consistent: in Oppianico sibi constare et superioribus consentire judiciis debuerunt,; so, with consentire,; : ut constare in vitae perpetuitate possimus nobismetipsis nec in ullo officio claudicare,; so, sibi (opp. titubare),: sibi et rei judicatae,: sibi,; ; cf.: constat idem omnibus sermo,.—
In the phrase ratio constat, mercantile t. t., the account agrees or is correct, is or proves right: auri ratio constat: aurum in aerario est,: quibus ratio impensarum constaret,was correct, accurately kept,.—
In postAug. prose, esp. in the younger Pliny, transf. from the sphere of business: mirum est, quam singulis diebus in urbe ratio aut constet aut constare videatur,; cf. ; 3, 18, 10; 2, 4, 4; 7, 6, 4; ; Just. praef. § 5: eam condicionem esse imperandi, ut non aliter ratio

constet, quam si uni reddatur, —

With the access. idea of firmness, to stand firm, to remain immovable, unchanging, steadfast, to abide, last, endure, persevere, etc. (very freq. in all perr. and styles).
In gen.: prius quam totis viribus fulta constaret hostium acies,; cf.: nec pugna deinde illis constare,: ut non color, non vultus ei constaret,; cf.: valetudo ei neque corporis neque animi constitit,; and: dum sanitas constabit,: non mentibus solum consipere, sed ne auribus quidem atque oculis satis constare poterant,; cf.: in ebrietate lingua non constat,: mente vix constare,; cf. ; : quā in sententia si constare voluissent,; cf. : numerus legionum constat,: ceteris exercitibus constare fidem,: utrimque fides constitit,kept their word,; .—Poet.: cum sint huc forsitan illa, Haec translata illuc; summā tamen omnia constant,i. e. the principal sum remains always the same,: postquam cuncta videt caelo constare sereno,every thing continues in unbroken serenity,: constitit in nullā qui fuit ante color,.—
In partic.
Milit. t. t., to stop, halt: multitudinem procul hostium constare videtur, Sisenn. ap. .—
Of facts, reports, etc., to be established, settled, certain, manifest, evident, well known: quae cum constent, perspicuum debet esse, etc.,: eorum quae constant exempla ponemus, horum quae dubia sunt, exempla adferemus, id. mv 1, 38, 68: quod nihil nobis constat,: cum et factum constet et nomen, qualia sint vocatur in dubium,; cf.: cum factum constat, sed a quo sit factum in controversiam venit,; and impers., with acc. and inf.: mihi multa agitanti constabat, paucorum civium egregiam virtutem cuncta patravisse,; cf.: quod omnibus constabat, hiemari in Gallia oportere,, and .—
Constat (constabat, constabit, etc., it is settled, established, undisputed, certain, well known, etc.), ; ; ; ; ; et saep.—So freq.: constat inter omnes, with acc. and inf., all agree, all are convinced: sed tum nimis inter omnis constabat neminem esse resalutatum,: quae propositio in se quiddam continet perspicuum et quod constare inter omnis necesse est, hanc velle approbare et firmare nihil attinet,in which all must agree, dub. (B. and K. stare); ; ; et saep.; cf. also: constare inter homines sapientissimos (for which, just after: omnium consensu sic esse judicatum),: inter suos,: inter augures, Liv 10, 6, 7 et saep.: cum de Magio constet,; cf.: de facto constat,; so with de, ; : etsi non satis mihi constiterat, cum aliquāne animi mei molestiā an potius, etc.,: nec satis certum constare apud animum poterat, utrum, etc.,: quid cuique sit opus constare decet,; so : quid porro quaerendum est? Factumne sit? At constat. A quo? At patet,; so absol., .—
Of a resolve.
Impers.: mihi (ei) constat, = certum est, it is my (his) fixed determination, I am determined, I am fully resolved (rare): mihi quidem constat, nec meam contumeliam, nec meorum ferre, Anton. ap. : neque satis Bruto neque tribunis militum constabat, quid agerent,were undecided,: ut nihil ei constet quod agat,.—
With the resolve as subject: animo constat sententia,: cum constitit consilium,when my mind was fully made up,.—
In gen., as opp. to that which has no existence, to exist, be, abide (esp. in Lucr.): (corpora) quoniam fragili naturā praedita constant,; ; et saep.: antiquissimi fere sunt, quorum quidem scripta constent,; : qui sine manibus et pedibus constare deum posse decreverunt, : si ipsa mens constare potest vacans corpore,.—
With ex, in, de, or the abl. (in Cic. only with ex; cf. Madv. ad ), to consist in or of, to be composed of, to rest upon something, etc.
With ex (very freq. in prose and poetry): fulminis ignem e parvis constare figuris,: homo ex animo constat et corpore,; id. Fin. l. l.: simplex (jus) e dulci constat olivo,: ea virtus, quae constat ex hominibus tuendis, et saep.—
With in and abl. (very rare): victoriam in earum cohortium virtute constare,; —*
With de: partus duplici de semine,.—
With abl. (freq. in Lucr. and Quint.): aeterno quia constant semine quaeque,; ; et saep.: agri campis, vineis, etc.,: constat tota oratio longioribus membris, brevioribus periodis,; et saep.: causa constat aut unius rei controversiā aut plurium,. omnis disciplina memoriā, . omne jus aut scripto aut moribus, et saep.—
Mercantile t. t., like our phrase, to stand at, i. e. to cost; constr. with abl.. gen., etc., of price (cf. Zumpt, Gr. § 444).
Lit.
With abl.: ut unae quadrigae Romae constiterint quadringentis milibus,; : filius auro,: navis gratis, (al. stare): HS. sex milibus tibi constant,, § 28: tanto nobis deliciae,: magno tibi,: parvo,; cf. gratis,; .—
With gen.: (ambulatiuncula) prope dimidio minoris constabit isto loco,; : quanti funus,; .—
With adv.: quod mihi constat carius, Lucil. ap. ; so, vilissime,. 6.—
With sup.: cujus area super HS. millies constitit,.—
Trop.: edocet, quanto detrimento et quot virorum fortium morte necesse sit constare victoriam,: odia constantia magno,: imperia pretio quolibet constant bene,.—Hence, constans, antis, P. a. (acc. to II. 1.), standing firm, firm, unchangeable, constant, immovable, uniform, fixed, stable, invariable (freq. and class.).
Lit.: mellis constantior est natura (sc. quam aquae),: constans uva contra tenorem unum algoris aestusve,: cujus in indomito constantior inguine nervus, Quam nova arbor, etc.,: cursus certi et constantes,; cf.: constans reversio stellarum (with conveniens),: constantissimus motus lunae,: nihil (mundo) motu constantius,; : constanti vultu graduque,: aetas, the mature age (of an adult), ; cf.: constans aetas, quae media dicitur,: aetate nondum constanti,: pax,firm, secure,: fides,: an ire comminus et certare pro Italiā constantius foret,safer,. —
Agreeing or accordant with itself, consistent, harmonious: quemadmodum in oratione constanti, sic in vitā omnia sint apta inter se et convenientia,: nihil intellego dici potuisse constantius,; cf.: incredibilia an inter se constantia,: rumores,: constans parum memoria hujus anni,: constans fama erat,; so, opinio,; —
Trop., intellectually or morally certain, sure, steadfast, constant, faithful, steady, unchanging: firmi et stabiles et constantes amici,; cf. : quem hominem? Levem? imo gravissimum. Mobilem? imo constantissimum,; cf. opp. varium, id. Fragm. ap. Spald.: pater amens at is quidem fuit omnium constantissimus,a very constant, steadfast man,; cf.: prudens et constans (testis),; and under adv.: (Helvidius Priscus) recti pervicax, constans adversus metus,: constans Fortuna tantum in levitate suā,; cf.: neque fidei constans, neque strenuus in perfidiā, Tac. H. 3, 57: constantior In vitiis, etc.,.—Adv.: constanter.
(Acc. to A.) Firmly, immovably, steadily, constantly: manere in suo statu,: constanter ac perpetuo placet consilium, Brut. ap. : vitiis gaudere constanter,.—Comp.: ut maneamus in perspicuis firmius et constantius,.—Sup.: impetus caeli constantissime conficiens vicissitudinis anniversarias,.—
Harmoniously, evenly, uniformly, consistently: constanter et aequaliter ingrediens oratio,: sibi constanter convenienterque dicere,; cf. ; in comp., ; in sup., ; ; so, hi constanter omnes nuntiaverunt,with one voice, unanimously,: aequabilius atque constantius sese res humanae haberent,: aequabilius atque constantius regere provincias,—
(Acc. to B.) Steadily, calmly, tranquilly, sedately: constanter ac non trepide pugnare,; cf. agere, Auct. B. Afr. 84: proelium inire,; : constanter et sedate ferre dolorem,: constanter et libere se gerere,: constanter prudenterque fit,: constanter delata beneficia (with judicio, considerate, and opp. repentino quodam impetu),.—Comp.: cetera exsequi,: acrius quam constantius proelium inire,.—Sup.: amicitias retinere,;

senses: to set up, establish, constitute, found
la:verb:constituo.html:
con-stĭtŭo, ŭi, ūtum, 3, v. a.
statuo
,
to cause to stand, put or lay down, to set, put, place, fix, station, deposit a person or thing somewhere (esp. firmly or immovably), etc. (the act. corresponding to consistere; class.).
In gen.
Prop.: hominem ante pedes Q. Manilii constituunt,: vobis (dīs) candentem taurum ante aras,: impedimenta,: reliquias praedonum contractas in urbibus,: unum aliquem lectorem,: velut in aliquā sublimi speculā constitutus,.—
Trop.: cum hujus vobis adulescentiam proposueritis, constituitote vobis ante oculos etiam hujus miseri senectutem,.—
Esp.,
Milit. t. t.
To station or post troops somewhere, to draw up, set in order: legionem Caesar passibus CC. ab eo tumulo constituit,: legiones pro castris in acie,fin.; 4, 35: aciem ordinesque intra silvas,: octo cohortes in fronte,: quod reliquum peditum erat, obliquo constituerunt colle,: naves ad latus apertum hostium,; cf.: naves aperto ac plano litore,fin.: naves nisi in alto,: subsidiarias (naves) in secundo ordine, Auct. B. Alex. 14, 3: classem apud Salamina exadversum Athenas,; cf. : praesidia in Rutenis provincialibus,.—Rarely of a single person: se constituere, to station or post one's self: dum se Gallus iterum eodem pacto constituere studet, Quadrig. ap. .—
In contrast with a march, to cause to halt: paulisper agmen constituit,; so, agmen,; : signa paulisper novitate rei,; so, signa,.—And trop.: si constituitur aliquando (narratio) ac non istā brevitate percurritur,.—
With the access. idea of preparation, to set up, erect, establish, found, build, construct, prepare, make, create, constitute (class. and very freq.).
Lit.: genus humanum, quorum omnia causā constituisse deos,: aggerem apparare, vineas agere, turres duas constituere coepit,: turres,: turrim,: castella ad extremas fossas,: vineas ac testudines,: locis certis horrea,: inane sepulcrum,: feralis cupressos,: ingentem quercum in tumulo,: pyras curvo in litore,: quattuor aras ad alta delubra dearum,; : aedem in foro geminis fratribus,: castra Romae, et saep.: oppidum,to found,; ; so, nova moenia,; cf.: moenia in Aside terrā,: domicilium sibi Magnesiae,: triplex Piraeei portus constitutus est,: hiberna omnium legionum in Belgis,: di primum homines humo excitatos celsos et erectos constituerunt,.—
Trop., to bring about, effect, establish, appoint, etc., freq. of judicial determinations, etc.: videte,

per deos immortalis, quod jus nobis, quam condicionem vobismet ipsis, quam denique civitati legem constituere velitis, to establish, : jus melius Sullanis praediis quam paternis,: judicium,: judicium de pecuniis repetundis,: judicium capitis in se,: controversiam,: quaestionem,; : ratiocinationem,: in hac accusatione comparandā constituendāque laborare,; and of persons, to designate, appoint, select, put forward, etc.: accusatorem,; (cf.: comparare accusatorem,): testis,: tutores pupillis, et saep.: nuper apud C. Orchivium collegam meum locus ab judicibus Fausto Sullae de pecuniis residuis non est constitutus,no trial of him was permitted,: reum statim fecit, utique ei locus primus constitueretur impetravit,: fidem,; cf. : concordiam,, D, 1: si utilitas amicitiam constituet, tollet eadem,: amicitiam tecum, (cf. § 25: amicitiae permultae comparantur): libertatem,: victoriam,: pacem (opp. bellum gerere),: quantum mali sibi ac liberis suis,.—

With the access. idea of ordering, contriving, to establish, fix, appoint, settle, order, manage; to confirm, regulate, arrange, dispose.
Lit.: Ti. et C. Gracchos plebem in agris publicis constituisse,to have established,; cf. : ibi futuros Helvetios, ubi eos Caesar constituisset,should assign them a permanent abode,: reges in civitate,; cf. : Commium regem ibi,: decemviralem potestatem in omnibus urbibus,; cf. : curatores legibus agrariis,; cf.: publice patronum huic causae,: regnum alicui,: composita et constituta res publica,; cf.: bene morata et bene constituta civitas,; so : civitates,to organize,: quis tibi concesserit ... reliquas utilitates in constituendis civitatibus ... a disertis ornateque dicentibus esse constitutas,: Chersoneso tali modo constituto,: res summā aequitate,; cf.: rem nummariam,: rem familiarem,.—
Trop.: ineuntis aetatis inscitia senum constituenda et regenda prudentiā est,; cf.: majores vestri majestatis constituendae gratiā bis Aventinum occupavere,; : jam perfectis constitutisque viribus,.— Pass. impers.: non tam sinistre constitutum est, ut non, etc., i. e. we are not so badly off as not, etc., .—Of persons: Athenaeum in maximā apud regem auctoritate gratiāque,: aliquem sibi quaestoris in loco,: in potestate aliquem,: constituuntur in honoribus, cum magistratus creantur,—
With the access. idea of limiting, fixing, allotting, to fix, appoint something (for or to something), to settle, agree upon, define, determine.
Lit.: propter dissensionem placuerat dividi thesauros finesque imperii singulis constitui,: summum pretium,; cf.: pretium frumento,: certam pecuniam proconsulibus,; : propria loca senatoribus,: diem nuptiis,; cf.: nuptias in hunc diem,: diem concilio,: diem colloquio,: posterum diem pugnae,fin.: negotio proximum diem,: certum tempus ei rei,: grandiorem aetatem ad consulatum,: tempus in posterum diem locumque,: postquam ad constitutam non venerat diem,: locus, tempus constitutum est,: modum credendi,: de numero pastorum alii angustius, alii laxius constituunt: ego in octogenas hirtas oves singulos pastores constitui, Atticus in centenas,.—
T. t. of the lang. of business, to accord, agree with one in a thing, to appoint, fix, to concert, agree upon, assent to (cf. Gron. Obss. p. 14 sq.); constr. aliquid cum aliquo, alicui, inter se, or with acc. only, or absol.
Cum aliquo: ubiea dies, quam constituerat cum legatis venit,: pactam et constitutam esse cum Manlio diem,: constitui cum quodam hospite, Me esse illum conventuram,: constitui cum hominibus, quo die mihi Messanae praesto essent,: cum aliquo, ut, etc., Aug. ap. ; cf. under P. a., B. 2.—
Alicui: L. Cincio HS. XXCD. constitui me curaturum Idibus Febr.,; : ubi nocturnae Numa constituebat amicae,; cf.: sane, inquit, vellem non constituissem, in Tusculanum me hodie venturum esse, Laelio,.—
With acc. only or absol.: vadimonia constituta,: de pecuniā constitutā,; : (Vaccenses) compositis inter se rebus in diem tertiam constituunt,: sic constituunt, sic condicunt,; .—Pass. impers.: Avillius, ut erat constitutum, simulat se aegrotare,.—
Trop.: constituendi sunt qui sint in amicitiā fines deligendi,: si forte quaereretur quae esset ars imperatoris, constituendum putarem principio, quis esset imperator: qui cum esset constitutus administrator quidam belli gerendi, tum adjungerem, etc. (for which, soon after, definire),; cf. C. 1. supra, and : nondum satis constitui molestiaene plus an voluptatis attulerit mihi Trebatius noster,: ut constitueret, honestum esse aliquid quod, etc.,: bona possessa non esse constitui,: de hoc Antigonus cum solus constituere non auderet, ad consilium retulit,.—
With the access. idea of resolving, to determine to do something, to take a resolution, to resolve, decide, determine.
With inf.: si quis mare Neptunum Cereremque vocare Constituit fruges,: cohortes duas in Nantuatibus collocare,: bellum cum Germanis gerere,: Romanorum adventum exspectare atque ibi decertare,: desciscere a rege,.—
With acc. and inf.: audio constitutum esse Pompeio et ejus consilio in Siciliam me mittere,. —
With interrog.-clause: quantum pecuniae quaeque civitas daret, Aristides delectus est, qui constitueret,. —
With ut: rus uti irem, jam heri constitueram,: constitueram, ut pridie Idus Aquini manerem,: constituimus inter nos ut ambulationem conficeremus,: Lentulus cum ceteris constituerant, uti, etc.,.—Hence, constĭtūtus, a, um, P. a.
Adj. (acc. to B.), constituted, arranged, disposed: bene constitutum corpus,: viri sapientes et bene naturā constituti,: quotus quisque philosophorum invenitur, qui sit ita moratus, ita animo ac vitā constitutus, ut ratio postulat,: qui integri sunt et sani et bene constituti de rebus domesticis,.—
(Acc. to C.) Fixed, established: cursus siderum,: discrimina (opp. fortuita),: jam confirmatae constitutaeque vocis,.—
Subst.: constĭtūtum, i, n.
(Acc. to B.) An institution, ordinance, law (mostly postclass.), Cod. Th. 1, 11, 5; 12, 41, 1.—
Trop.: cum videas ordinem rerum et naturam per constituta procedere,according to established laws,.—
(Acc. to D. 1. b.) An agreement, appointment, accommodation; a compact (in good prose): ante rem quaeruntur, quae talia sunt, apparatus, conloquia, locus, constitutum, convivium,; so absol., ; : rescripsit constitutum se cum eo habere,: constitutum factum esse cum servis, ut venirent, etc.,; and humorously: si quod constitutum cum podagra habes, fac ut in alium diem differas, ; so, ad constitutum venire,; : se proripu it,; and without a verb,; (but in , the better read. is consili).

Antiq., and the authors there cited (freq. in all periods and species of composition): qui recte consulat, consul cluat, Att. ap. Müll.; ; ; : consul ordinarius, one who entered on his office at the regular time, viz. on the first of January; opp. consul suffectus, one chosen in the course of the year in the place of one who had died, or, after the time of the emperors, as a mere honorary title; v. ordinarius and sufficio: consul designatus, consul elect (so called in the interval between election, at the beginning of August, and entrance on his duties, on the 1st of January), v. designo: consul major, one who had the largest number of votes, or with whom the Fasces were, or one who was oldest (acc. to Nieb., orig. he who was of noble origin); cf. Fest. s. v. majorem consulem, p. 161, 31 Müll.; after the Lex Julia,who had most children,: consulem creare,; : dicere,: facere,; : sufficere,: declarare,: renuntiare,: aliquem consulem designare,: esse pro consule, In reference to the expression bis, iterum, ter, quater, etc.; tertio or tertium, etc, consul, v. the words bis, iterum, etc., and cf. and 6.—

Sing., as collective term for the magistracy, the consuls, when the office is in view rather than the persons: quod populus in se jus dederit, eo consulem usurum; non ipsos (sc. consules) libidinem ac licentiam suam pro lege habituros, Weissenb. ad loc.: legatisque ad consulem missis, Heerw. ad loc.: aliter sine populi jussu nullius earum rerum consuli jus est,.—
Meton.

Absol.: quid nunc? etiam consulis? do you still deliberate, i. e. hesitate? ; cf. Speng.: ne quid in consulendo adversi eveniat, Cato ap. : consulto opus est,there is need of deliberation,: dum tempus consulendi est,: satis facere consulentibus,: ut omnium rerum vobis ad consulendum potestas esset,: ut tot uno tempore motibus animi turbati trepidarent magis quam consulerent,: praesidium consulenti curiae, et saep.—
With in and acc.: consulere in longitudinem,to take thought for the future,: in commune,for the common good,; ; ; ; ; and in the same sense: in medium,; ; ; : in unum,; : in publicum (opp. suscipere proprias simultates),; .—
With de and abl.: bello confecto de Rhodiis consultum est,; so, de communibus negotiis,: de salute suorum,: omnibus de rebus,.—
With ut or ne: consulere vivi ac prospicere debemus, ut illorum (liberorum) solitudo munita sit,: tu ne qua manus se attollere nobis A tergo possit, custodi et consule longe,.—Impers.: ut urbi ... satis esset praesidii, consultum atque provisum est,: ne deficerent, consulendum esse,.—
Esp., consulere alicui or alicui rei, to take care for some person or thing, to be mindful of, take care of, look to, have regard for, to counsel or consult for: tuae rei bene consulere cupio,: quid me fiat, parvi pendis, dum illi consulas,: qui parti civium consulunt, partem neglegunt,: consulere eorum commodis et utilitati salutique

servire, ; so, famae, pudicitiae tuae,: dignitati meae,: suae vitae,: receptui sibi,: reipublicae juxta ac sibi,; ; : timori magis quam religioni,; cf.: magis irae quam famae,: qui mi consultum optime velit esse,: mi ires consultum male? to counsel evil or badly, ; so, male patriae,; .—With si: melius consulet (sibi), si, etc.,.—

Act.
Consulere aliquem (or aliquid), to consult with one, to ask his opinion or advice, to ask counsel of, to consult, question (for the sake of advice).
In gen.: cum te consuluissem, quid mihi faciendum esse censeres,: te, qui philosophum audis,: Apellem tragoedum, uter, etc.,—Of inanim. objects: speculum suum,; cf.: spectatas undas, quid se deceat,: nares, an olerent aera Corinthōn,: diem de gemmis, etc.,: animum nostrum,: aures meas,: suas vires,—With two accs.: ibo et consulam hanc rem amicos, quid faciundum censeant,: nec te id consulo,: consulere prudentiorem coepi aetates tabularum,.—Freq.,
Esp. as t. t.
In the lang. of religion, to consult a deity, an oracle, omens, etc.: Apollinem de re,: deum consuluit auguriis, quae suscipienda essent,: deos hominum fibris,: Phoebi oracula,; : Tiresiam conjectorem,: haruspicem,; ; : vates nunc extis, nunc per aves,: Cumaeam anum,: avem primum visam augur,: spirantia exta,; so, trepidantia exta,: sacras sortes,: Etrusci haruspices male consulentes,.—Pass. impers.: si publice consuletur ... sin privatim,. —With dependent question: senatus pontificum collegium consuli jussit, num omne id aurum in ludos consumi necessum esset,: consulti per ludibrium pontifices, an concepto necdum edito partu rite nuberet,.—
In judic. lang., to ask advice of a lawyer, to consult, etc.: quam inanes domus eorum omnium, qui de jure civili consuli solent,: consuli quidem te a Caesare scribis: sed ego tibi ab illo consuli mallem,: si jus consuleres, peritissimus,: munus hoc eorum qui consuluntur,i. e. who are skilled in the law,; so .— With dependent question: consulens eum, an seni jam testato suaderet ordinare suprema judicia,.—The formula usual in asking advice was, licet consulere? ; cf. .—
In publicists' lang., to take counsel with the competent authorities, to consult: Quirites, utrum, etc.,; so, senatum,: senatum de foedere,; 62, 10: populum de ejus morte,: plebem in omnia (tribuni),—
Aliquid.
To take counsel or deliberate upon something, to consider: est consulere quiddam quod tecum volo,; : rem delatam consulere ordine non licuit,; so, consulere et explorare rem,: consulis rem nulli obscuram,: bis repulsi Galli quid agant consulunt,.—
To advise something, to give advice: tun' consulis quicquam?; .—Absol.: ab re consulit blandiloquentulus,advises to his hurt,.
Sometimes meton. (causa pro effectu).
To take a resolution, resolve, conclude, determine.
Neutr.; constr. absol. or with de aliquo or in aliquem: de nullis quam de vobis infestius aut inimicius consuluerunt,; so, de perfugis gravius quam de fugitivis,: in humiliores libidinose crudeliterque consulebatur,; so, crudeliter in deditos victosque,; cf. . —
Act.: quid in concilio consuluistis?: animum ego inducam tamen, ut illud, quod tuam in rem bene conducat, consulam,: ne quid gravius de salute tuā consulas, Cael. ap. : pessime istuc in te atque in illum consulis,: quae reges irā inpulsi male consuluerint,: nisi quod de uxore potuit honestius consuli,.—Pass. impers.: aliter mihi de illis ac de me ipso consulendum est,.—
With the access. idea of judging, in the connection boni, optimi aliquid consulere, to excuse, take in good part, interpret favorably; be contented, pleased, or satisfied with: sit consul a consulendo vel a judicando: nam et hoc consulere veteres vocaverunt, unde adhuc remanet illud Rogat boni consulas, id est bonum judices,; cf. Paul. ex Müll.: nemo hoc rex ausus est facere, eane fieri bonis, bono genere gnatis boni consulitis? Cato ap. : boni consulendum, Müll.: tu haec quaeso consule missa boni,; cf. ; so, nostrum laborem,; : hoc munus,; ; ; ; : quaerebat argentum avaritia: boni consuluit interim invenisse minium, § 4; 8, 16, 17, § 44: boni et optimi consulere,.— Hence,
consultus, a, um, P. a.
Well considered or weighed, deliberated upon, maturely pondered: bene consultum consilium surripitur saepissume, si minus, etc.,: ipsi omnia, quorum negotium est, consulta ad nos et exquisita deferunt,: neque eam usquam invenio, neque quo eam, neque quā quaeram consultum'st, I know neither, etc., : operā consultā,with mature reflection,; in the same sense, consulto consilio,: consultius est huic poenalem quoque stipulationem subjungere,it is better. more advantageous,.—
(Acc. to I. B. 1.) Knowing, skilful, experienced, practised, esp. in law; skilled or learned in the law: non ille magis juris consultus quam justitiae fuit,: juris atque eloquentiae,: consultissimus vir omnis divini atque humani juris,; cf. : insanientis sapientiae,: universae disciplinae,.—Hence, subst.: consultus, i, m., a lawyer: tu consultus modo rusticus,; ; ; .— Esp. with juris, often written as one word, jūrisconsultus, i, m., v. h. v.—Absol.: ut natura non disciplinā consultus esse videatur,: consultorum alterum disertissimum, disertorum alterum consultissimum fuisse,: consultiores sibimet videntur Deo,.—
Subst.: consultum, i, n.
(Acc. to I. B. 1. b.) A consultation, inquiry of a deity: Sostratus (sacerdos) ubi laeta et congruentia exta magnisque consultis annuere deam videt, etc.,.—
(Acc. to II.) A decree, decision, resolution, plan; so first, Senatus consultum, or in one word, Senatusconsul-tum, a decree of the Senate (most freq. in all periods; the senatus consulta were not, like the plebiscita, the supreme law of the republic; but under the emperors, all new laws took this form, v. esp. Sandars, Introd., § 15; 1, 2, 5),; : senatus consultum est quod senatus jubet atque constituit, nam cum auctus esset populus Romanus ... aequum visum est senatum vice populi consuli,; for which, consulta Patrum,. —Of a decree of the Sicilian council: ne senatus consultum Siculi homines facere possent,.—Also in other connections: facta et consulta fortium et sapientium,; cf.: facta consultaque Alexandri, Dietsch: consulta et decreta,: consulta sese omnia cum illo integra habere,all objects of consultation, plans,; cf.: ab occultis cavendum hominibus consultisque,plans,; and: approbare collegam consulta,: dum consulta petis,responses, oracles, divinations,: tua magna,decisions,; so, mollia,: mala,: ex consulto factum,purposely, voluntarily,.—Hence, adv., considerately, deliberately, designedly, on purpose.
Form consultō (class. in prose and poetry): utrum perturbatione aliquā animi an consulto et cogitata fiat injuria,; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; ; * —
Form consultē (mostly ante- and post-class.): qui consulte, docte atque astute cavet,: caute atque consulte gesta,; .—Comp., ; . —Sup., .

With acc.: quid illaec illic in consilio duae secreto consultant?: ad haec consultanda procurandaque,: ad eam rem consultandam,; ; : cum in senatu res major quaepiam consultata est,.—

In gen. (very freq. in all periods, esp. in prose): exercitatio ex quā consuetudo gignitur,: dicunt ... consuetudine quasi alteram naturam effici,: ad parentium consuetudinem moremque deducimur,; ; : majorum,; cf. : Siculorum ceterorumque Graecorum,; ; ; cf. : eorum dierum,: non est meae consuetudinis rationem reddere, etc.,: con

With prepp., ex consuetudine, pro consuetudine, and absol. consuetudine, according to or from custom, by or from habit, in a usual or customary manner, etc.: Germani celeriter ex consuetudine suā phalange factā impetus gladiorum exceperunt,; so with ex, ; ; ; : pro meā consuetudine,according to my custom,: consuetudine suā Caesar sex legiones expeditas ducebat,; : consuetudine animus rursus te huc inducet,: huc cum se consuetudine reclinaverunt,; so ; —Less freq.: praeter consuetudinem, contrary to experience, unexpectedly (opp. praeter naturam), : plures praeter consuetudinem armatos apparere,contrary to custom,; cf.: contra consuetudinem,: supra consuetudinem,.—

Customary right, usage as a common law: (jus) constat ex his partibus: naturā, lege, consuetudine, judicato ... consuetudine jus est id, quod sine lege aeque ac si legitimum sit, usitatum est,; : consuetudine jus esse putatur id, quod voluntate omnium sine lege vetustas comprobavit,; Varr. ap. ; ; ; .—
In gram. (instead of consuetudo loquendi; cf. supra), a usage or idiom of language, in 8th and 9th books on almost every page; ; ; ; .—Hence,
In Col. for language in gen.: consuetudini Latinae oeconomicum Xenophontis tradere,, praef. § 7: nostra (opp. Graeca),.—
Social intercourse, companionship, familiarity, conversation (freq. and class; in an honorable sense most freq. in Cic.).
In gen.: (Deiotarus) cum hominibus nostris consuetudines, amicitias, res rationesque jungebat,; so in plur.: victūs cum multis,; and in sing.: victūs,: domesticus usus et consuetudo est alicui cum aliquo,; cf. : consuetudine conjuncti inter nos sumus,: consuetudine ac familiaritate,; so with familiaritas,: dare se in consuetudinem,: insinuare in alicujus consuetudinem,; cf.: immergere se in consuetudinem alicujus,: epistularum,epistolary correspondence,: nutrimentorum,community,.—
In partic., intercourse in love, in an honorable, and more freq. in a dishonorable sense, a love affair, an amour, love intrique, illicit intercourse, ; ; ; ; ; ; ; and 7; ; — So also freq.: consuetudo stupri,; ; ; .
